chunks: How a servo works inside. The question: How does it work?
Inside a hobby servo are a small motor, gears, a position sensor on the output shaft, and a control chip. You send a pulse whose width says the angle you want.
The chip reads the sensor to learn the actual angle, then runs the motor in whichever direction closes the gap. It stops when the two agree.
Imagine steering a boat toward a lighthouse. The lighthouse is the target, and your compass reading is the sensor.
If the lighthouse is far off to the left, you turn the wheel hard left. As you line up, you ease the wheel back toward straight.
When you point right at it, you hold the wheel still. A servo's chip does the same with the motor, many times a second.
Each character is 0. 5 milliseconds, so the frame shown is 20 milliseconds. The three signals are three different commands: widths of 1. 0, 1. 5 and 2. 0 milliseconds.
The servo ignores the frame period and just times how long the line stays high.
Pulse width: how long the signal stays high in each pulse. For a hobby servo it is about 1 to 2 milliseconds, sent every 20 milliseconds, and it sets the target angle.
Potentiometer: a variable resistor on the output shaft. Its voltage tells the chip the angle. Error: target angle minus actual angle.
H-bridge: the switches that let the chip run the motor either way. Deadband: a tiny error range where the chip does nothing, so the motor does not twitch back and forth.
Suppose 1. 0 milliseconds means 0 degrees and 2. 0 milliseconds means 180 degrees. You send 1. 5 milliseconds, so the target is 90 degrees.
The potentiometer says the shaft is at 60 degrees, so the error is +30 degrees and the chip drives the motor forward.
At 85 degrees the error is only 5 degrees, so the drive is gentler. At about 90 degrees the error falls inside the deadband and the drive stops. That is the whole idea.
"The servo measures the width of a 1 to 2 milliseconds pulse that arrives every 20 milliseconds and treats it as a target angle.
A potentiometer on the output shaft reports the actual angle.
The control chip subtracts them to get an error and drives an H-bridge so the motor turns toward the target, roughly proportional to the error, stopping inside a small deadband.
A gearbox trades motor speed for torque. Push on the shaft and the error returns, so it pushes back."
